title: Don Quixote, pages 1–12
sub: Built to match tonight's reading guide. Part 1 is the things to look for while reading; Part 2 is the clues to save for Friday's write-up.
cite: Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes, Core Classics abridged for young readers
note: Twenty questions, under ten minutes. The questions and the answers are shuffled every time, so running it twice is not the same quiz twice. Get one wrong and a hint names the page — that page number is what goes on your guide.
bigq: Is Don Quixote simply imagining adventures, or does he believe they are real? Use three examples from the reading and explain your judgment.

groups.name: Part 1
groups.blurb: The things your reading guide tells you to look for, in fourteen questions.

groups.name: Part 2
groups.blurb: What he thinks he sees against what is really there — the clues you are collecting for the big question.

groups.name: Extra
groups.blurb: Not part of tonight's ten minutes. The toolkit rules and the Week 1 words, for when you want them.

items.q: Where does the story take place?
opts: In a village in the province of La Mancha, in Spain
In the city of Seville, on the southern coast of Spain
In a castle in the mountains above a village in Spain
On a farm in the hills of Portugal, close to the border
items.hint: The very first sentence names the province. He later puts that name into his own.
items.why: “Once upon a time there lived in a village in Spain, in the province of La Mancha.”

items.q: Who is the main character, and who lives in his house?
opts: A young knight called Don Belianis, who lives all alone in a great castle in the hills
A gentleman called Quixania, with a housekeeper, a niece and a handyman
A farmer called Amadis of Gaul, who lives with his wife and his children
A soldier called Rocinante, who lives with his elderly mother and sister
items.hint: His household is three people, and the niece is under twenty.
items.why: “His name was Quixania.” His household was an elderly housekeeper, a niece under twenty, and a handyman.

items.q: What was he like at the start of the story?
opts: A wealthy young lord with a large household of servants, horses and dogs
About fifty, thin but tough, an early riser and a great lover of hunting
A young and strong man who had already been trained as a knight
A soldier who had fought in many real battles for the king
items.hint: He was thin, with a lean face, and he was a very early riser.
items.why: “About fifty, thin, but tough of body, with a lean face, a very early riser, and a great lover of hunting.”

items.q: What kind of books does he love, and what do they do to him?
opts: Histories of the kings of Spain; he sets off to join the king's army at once
Romances of chivalry; he gives up hunting and his judgment becomes warped
Books of poetry; he begins writing verses about his own neighborhood
Books about farming; he decides to grow more crops than ever before
items.hint: They are stories about knights. He even sold good cropland to buy more of them.
items.why: Romances of chivalry. He lost interest in hunting, neglected his daily concerns, and his judgment became “so warped.”

items.q: What does he decide to become?
opts: A writer of romances about knights and their adventures
A soldier in the king's army, fighting in real battles
A knight, riding about the world setting wrongs right
A farmer with far more cropland than he had before
items.hint: He wanted to do what the men in his books did, and go out seeking adventures.
items.why: He resolved “to become a knight himself and ride about the world setting wrongs right and seeking adventures.”

items.q: He polished up his ancestors' old armor. What was missing from it?
opts: A sword, so he had to borrow one from a neighbor
A shield, which had been lost many years before
Gloves, without which he could not hold his lance
A helmet — he had only a simple steel cap
items.hint: The armor had lain for ages in a corner, covered with dust and rust. One piece only half did the job.
items.why: “There was no helmet, only a simple steel cap,” so he made a visor out of cardboard to go with it.

items.q: What happened when he tested his cardboard visor?
opts: His sword broke in half against the hard cardboard
He destroyed it with one stroke of his sword
It held up perfectly well and he was delighted
He decided it was too risky and did not test it
items.hint: He wanted to know whether it would resist cuts, so he drew his sword and struck it.
items.why: “He made a stroke at it and in one instant demolished” the work of a whole week.

items.q: What did he do about the visor after that?
opts: He gave up on cardboard and bought a real helmet in the village
He lined the cardboard with iron and did not test it again
He borrowed a proper helmet from one of his neighbors
He tested a second one and this time it held together
items.hint: He made it stronger, then made very sure he never found out whether it was strong enough.
items.why: He lined it with strips of iron and “declared his new visor was sufficiently strong, without risking any more experiments on it.”

items.q: What does he name his horse, and what is the horse really like?
opts: Bucephalus; really a fine young charger that he had bought
Rocinante; really an old horse that is skin and bone
Dulcinea; really a strong horse he had raised himself
Amadis; really a horse he borrowed from a neighbor
items.hint: It had as many points as a mariner's compass, but he thought it finer than the famous horse of Alexander.
items.why: Rocinante. Really skin and bone; to him, a charger superior to the Bucephalus of Alexander. He took four days to choose the name.

items.q: What new name does he give himself, and why that one?
opts: Don Belianis of Spain, to honor the king that he serves
Don Quixote de la Mancha, to honor his home region
Don Amadis of Gaul, to honor the knight he admires
Don Quixote of Toboso, to honor the lady he loves
items.hint: It took him eight days more. He copied the valiant Amadis, who added the name of his country to his own.
items.why: Don Quixote, enlarged to Don Quixote de la Mancha, so that he “made clear his origin and honored his country by adopting its name.”

items.q: Who is Dulcinea del Toboso really?
opts: A princess he had once met at the court of the king of Spain
A farmer's daughter called Aldonza Lorenzo
A lady who had written to him about the books he loved
His niece, who was under twenty and lived in his house
items.hint: She lived in his own neighborhood, and she did not seem to know or care anything about him.
items.why: Aldonza Lorenzo, a good-looking farmer's daughter. He renamed her Dulcinea del Toboso because she came from Toboso.

items.q: Why does he almost turn back soon after leaving home?
opts: He remembered he had left his shield hanging up in his hall
He remembered he had never been dubbed a knight
He realised that Rocinante was too old for the journey
He saw that his visor was still only cardboard inside
items.hint: By the laws of chivalry he could wear only white armor and carry no device until he had earned one.
items.why: He had not been dubbed a knight in the proper form. He decided to get knighted by the first knight he met.

items.q: Which road does Don Quixote take?
opts: The widest and busiest road that he could find
The road leading back toward his own village
The road that led south in the direction of Seville
Whichever road his horse chose
items.hint: He thought that letting it happen this way was the true spirit of adventure.
items.why: “He allowed his horse to follow whatever road it pleased, considering this to be the true spirit of adventure.”

items.q: The last page of tonight's reading is a full-page picture. What does it show?
opts: Don Quixote fighting off the angry mule drivers with his shield
Don Quixote kneeling as the innkeeper dubs him a knight
Don Quixote marching up and down in the bright moonlight
Don Quixote riding away from the inn at first light
items.hint: Look at the caption printed under the picture. He is guarding something, all night long.
items.why: The caption reads: “For hours he marched up and down in the bright moonlight.” He is watching his armor.

items.q: He reaches an inn at nightfall. What does he think it is?
opts: A monastery where the monks would give him food and a bed for the night
A castle with four towers, silver spires, a drawbridge and a moat
A shepherd's hut of the kind he had been looking for all day
The great stone house of a giant he would have to fight
items.hint: Everything he saw was tinted and transformed by the nonsense he had gathered from his books.
items.why: He “at once pictured this inn as a castle with four towers, spires of polished silver, a drawbridge and moat.” Believed: a castle. Really: an inn. Page 8.

items.q: Two young women were standing by the door. What does he take them for?
opts: Servants he could send inside to announce him
Prisoners of the lord of the castle, in need of rescue
Two beautiful damsels
Travellers he ought to warn about robbers on the road
items.hint: They were on their way to Seville and stopping for the night, and he spoke to them as though they were highborn ladies.
items.why: They “appeared to him to be two beautiful damsels.” Really: two travellers, who were alarmed by him. Page 8.

items.q: A pig-driver blew a horn to call his herd in from a field. What does Don Quixote make of it?
opts: A warning that robbers were somewhere near
A bell calling the guests in to their supper
A trumpet announcing his arrival
A church bell ringing in a village nearby
items.hint: He had been waiting at the door of what he thought was a castle, expecting a dwarf or a page to do exactly this.
items.why: “At once Don Quixote recognized this as the signal of his arrival.” Believed: his herald. Really: a man calling pigs. Page 8.

items.q: Who does he ask to make him a knight, and what does that man really think of him?
opts: A passing knight, who agrees because he admires his courage
The landlord, who can see he is mad and plays along
A priest at the chapel, who refuses him at first
The lord of the castle, who believes every word he says
items.hint: He fell on his knees and begged in very flowery language. The man he asked knew the romances well and had guests to entertain.
items.why: The landlord “readily made out the kind of madness from which the stranger suffered” and played along to amuse himself and his guests.

items.q: Where does he put his armor for the night, and why not in the chapel?
opts: In the stable, because the chapel had been locked up for the night
In a trough in the yard, because the chapel had been demolished
On the altar, because the host led him there himself
In his room, because the host said the yard was not safe
items.hint: The host had an answer ready, and said such a thing was allowed in cases of necessity.
items.why: The chapel “had recently been demolished so that it might be rebuilt,” so he put his armor in a trough in one of the yards.

items.q: Two mule drivers came to move his armor. What does what he did tell you about him?
opts: He let them take it, which shows he knew the vigil was only a game
He knocked them out with his lance, which shows he meant it
He called the landlord, which shows he was afraid of them
He hid and watched, which shows he was only pretending
items.hint: They only wanted to fetch water for their mules. The landlord had to stop the fight by telling their friends he was a madman.
items.why: He was not pretending. He gave the first a thwack on the head with his lance and the second met the same fate, and the landlord had to call the drivers off by telling them he was a madman. Acting on a belief, at real cost to real people, is the strongest evidence you have.

items.q: In RACES, what does the C step ask you to do?
opts: Compare this book with another story that you have read
Give specific evidence and the printed page numbers
Check your spelling and your punctuation carefully
Copy out the question at the top of your answer
items.hint: Look at the toolkit table on page 2 of your guide. It is the step that puts numbers in your answer.
items.why: Cite: “Give specific evidence and printed page numbers. Include the number of examples requested.”

items.q: The big question asks for three examples. How many do you have to cite?
opts: One good one is enough if you explain it well
Two, with the third saved for the final essay
Three
As many as you can fit on the page
items.hint: The Cite row says to include the number of examples requested. The evidence table has exactly that many rows.
items.why: Three. The guide says to include the number of examples requested, and the table gives you three rows for them.

items.q: When should you use quotation marks?
opts: Whenever you mention something that happened in the book
Only when you copy the author's exact words
Every time that you give a page number
Whenever you write about a character's speech
items.hint: Your detective habits say this in one line, just after the part about paraphrasing.
items.why: “Use quotation marks only when you copy the author's exact words.”

items.q: You put something from the book into your own words. Do you still need a page number?
opts: No, page numbers are only needed for direct quotations
Only if the detail comes from the home reading
Only if your teacher asks you for one
Yes — a paraphrase still needs a page citation
items.hint: This is the line directly before the one about quotation marks.
items.why: “A paraphrase needs a page citation.” Putting it in your own words does not make it yours.

items.q: Which of these is a theme, rather than just a topic?
opts: Imagination, and what it can do to a person's mind
Believing something strongly does not make it true
The adventures of a man who reads too many books
Knights, and the stories people tell about them
items.hint: Your guide says a theme is a complete message about life, not a single word.
items.why: A theme is “a complete message about life, rather than a single topic word.” The others are topics or a plot summary.

items.q: Your detective habits say to explain a detail. What does that mean?
opts: Retell what happened in as much detail as you possibly can
Say what it shows, rather than only saying what happened
Describe what the picture on the page looks like
Write down every word that the character said
items.hint: The guide puts it as a contrast: explain a detail instead of doing one other thing.
items.why: “Explain a detail instead of only retelling it.” That is exactly what the third column of the evidence table is for.

items.q: Your Week 1 page defines chivalry. What is it?
opts: A code of conduct associated with knights
The armor and weapons a knight carried into battle
A long journey made on horseback in search of adventure
The ceremony in which a man is made a knight
items.hint: Your guide gives it in a few words under “Words for the journey.”
items.why: “chivalry = a code of conduct associated with knights.”

items.q: Your Week 1 page defines squire. What is one?
opts: A knight who has won a great many battles
A nobleman who owns a great deal of land
A knight's helper
A horse trained to carry a knight in armor
items.hint: You have not met one yet in pages 1 to 12. Watch for the man who takes this job later on.
items.why: “squire = a knight's helper.” Sancho Panza takes that role further into the book.

items.q: Your Week 1 page defines irony. What is it?
opts: A meaningful contrast between expectation and reality
A funny remark made at somebody else's expense in a story
A story that teaches a lesson about life
A word that sounds like the thing it describes
items.hint: It is about the gap between what somebody expects and what is really so. This whole book runs on it.
items.why: “irony = a meaningful contrast between expectation and reality.”

items.q: Which moment in pages 1–12 is the best example of irony?
opts: He spends four whole days deciding what he ought to call his horse
He sells good cropland so that he can buy himself more books
He sets out before daybreak so that nobody will see him go
He destroys his own visor, rebuilds it, then refuses to test it
items.hint: Look at what he does with the visor after he lines the cardboard with iron. He declares it strong without risking any more experiments.
items.why: He proved the visor useless with one stroke, then made certain never to prove it again. He expects to be a great knight; the reality is cardboard and strips of iron. Page 4.
